standard_prerequisites.name: Set-quotients by a generated equivalence relation
standard_prerequisites.statement: A set-quotient may be presented by relations, and a map out of it is defined by quotient recursion once the map respects the generating relations.
standard_prerequisites.use: The theorem defines F'(A) as such a quotient at source line 1639, and the proof defines multiplication and inversion on it by quotient recursion at lines 1651 and 1659.

standard_prerequisites.name: Lists over a type form a monoid
standard_prerequisites.statement: lst B with concatenation and the empty list is a monoid, and it has a recursion principle by list induction.
standard_prerequisites.use: The monoid structure of lst(A+A) is what descends to the quotient at source line 1650, and list induction is used at lines 1662-1669.

standard_prerequisites.name: Quotient induction and double quotient recursion
standard_prerequisites.statement: To prove a family of propositions over a set-quotient it suffices to prove it on representatives, and a binary operation may be defined by double quotient recursion when it respects the relation in each variable.
standard_prerequisites.use: Double quotient recursion defines the multiplication at source line 1651 and quotient induction reduces the inverse law to lists at line 1662.

core_obligations: Define F'(A) as the set-quotient of lst(A+A) by the two cancellation relations, and show it is a group: descend the monoid structure of lists to the quotient by double quotient recursion, then prove associativity and the unit laws by quotient induction (source lines 1649-1652).

Define reverse : lst B -> lst B by list recursion and use it, together with the switch of the two copies of A, to define the inverse i on F'(A) by quotient recursion, checking that the relations are preserved (source lines 1654-1660).

Prove i(x) `ct` x = e for all x : F'(A): reduce to x of the form q(ell) by quotient induction, then do list induction, carrying out the two cases at lines 1663-1670 (the second case using the inductive hypothesis), and note the evident lemmas about concatenation that are omitted (source line 1671).

For the universal property, send a : A to the first copy and use the group structure of G to get a monoid homomorphism lst(A+A) -> G, check it respects the relations so that it descends to F'(A) -> G, and verify it is the unique group homomorphism restricting to f (source lines 1674-1677).

proof_roadmap.step: Show that F'(A) is a group: descend the monoid structure and prove the laws by quotient induction.
Define reverse and hence the inverse by quotient recursion, checking compatibility with the relations.
Prove the inverse law by quotient induction followed by list induction, with concatenation lemmas omitted.
Verify the universal property by descending a monoid homomorphism from lists and checking uniqueness.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the unlabelled theorem at source lines 1638-1647, Theorem 6.11.7: the set-quotient of lst(A+A) by the two cancellation relations is again the free group on A. The author's 31-line proof (source lines 1648-1678) is a full construction of the group structure on a quotient, not a citation of the abstract universal property: the multiplication is defined by double quotient recursion and the unit and associativity laws are proved by quotient induction (lines 1650-1652), the inverse is built from a reverse operation on lists and checked against the relations (lines 1654-1660), and the inverse law i(x) `ct` x = e is reduced first by quotient induction and then by list induction, with the inductive case carried out explicitly at lines 1663-1670 and further concatenation lemmas deliberately omitted at line 1671. The final universal property is then checked on the quotient rather than assumed.
